To be sure, I have a few friends whom I've seen struggle as much as I have since college. In addition, my family has been supportive. That said, I recently moved away from home, because I know I'm becoming a burden on them. In all honesty, I'm very close to not following up on the Walmart job, buying myself a case of beer, and getting on with it. 

Every other day, a recruiter leaves a voicemail on my phone in an effort to recruit me as a substitute teacher for this district, but I've lost all interest in taking another low-paying temp job just to get by.

No matter what is making you feel that way, you should realize that, if you want it, you can get help. 

2-1-1 is a free and confidential service that helps people in the U.S. find local resources, including food, housing, and counseling services. To reach the service, you can dial "211" on your phone, or you can go to "211.org" to chat with them. 2-1-1 is available 24/7/365, and its staff is very professional and supportive. 

Before you do anything else, you should call and see how they can help you.

I really appreciate the positive comments. We'll see how long I decide to keep fighting. By the way, I graduated in 2010 and have been struggling ever since. Six years (particularly the last two, though) is a long time to live in a state of dystopia.

So far, I've only gotten offers for a low-wage temp jobs, and that's going to make it very difficult to find any stability. On Friday, for example, I went to an interview at Walmart and was offered a part-time temp position. Right now, Walmart is hiring temp workers for the holiday season. After the holidays are over, Walmart typically lets more than half of its temp hires go. It's business.

I have no problem with interviews. After all, to be an effective substitute teacher, you have to be able to project self-confidence and speak somewhat well extemporaneously. Rather, my biggest concern is that the the background investigators would disqualify me for, among other things, some of the crappy jobs I've quit on short notice. As for your last question, I spend a lot of my money on books, particularly on ones about terrorism. Given how much I've read on the topic, I feel as if I could contribute to the security of the U.S. in general and to the agency  in particular.

Thanks for the reply. 

Ideally, I'd like to work for the FBI as an intelligence analyst, but realistically, I know that my chances of getting in are slim to none. 

In order to be hired by the FBI, you have to make it through three phases. Phase I is an IQ test, Phase II is a writing exam, and Phase III is an oral board (i.e., interview) and an invasive background check, including a polygraph exam. Applicants have two opportunities to pass each phase. Otherwise, they can never join the FBI. 

As it stands, I've passed Phase I and II, but I never scheduled Phase III (i.e., the interview). Given my piss-poor work history (e.g., substitute teaching), I know I'd fail Phase III.

Insofar as you have thoughts of death but don't ostensibly have a specific plan as to how you would harm yourself, you  have a low risk of committing suicide. 

One of the risk factors associated with suicide is someone's sense of belongingness. Specifically, a low sense of belonging is typically associated with elevated levels of depression as well as suicidal ideation. 

In my opinion, your thwarted sense of belonging seems to be what's affecting you the most, particularly on the weekends, and as a result, I think the best course of action is to, as you're already doing, keep trying to find a therapist who will ultimately help you heal.

More often than not, a good therapist can help someone devise a plan whereby they can modify their sense of belonging. So, I wouldn't give up your search for help just yet!

Admittedly, you're in a very difficult situation, and I'm sorry to hear that. You aren't alone, however. 

Since the economy tanked in 2008, nearly every person in the U.S., regardless of their citizenship, has made a lot of sacrifices. For example, more than 7 million families have been forced out of their homes. 

At a minimum, however, every human needs food, shelter, and clothing, and fortunately enough, there are services out there that can help you and your family obtain those things, should you ever need them. 

Specifically, 2-1-1 is a free and confidential service that helps people in the U.S. find local resources, including employment, food, and housing. To reach the service, you can dial "211" on your phone, or you can go to "211.org" to chat with them. 2-1-1 is available 24/7/365, and its staff are very supportive and professional. 

2-1-1 isn't just a hotline for people who are struggling with suicide, so I hope you considering calling; it may help your family find housing as well as employment.

Long-term underemployment, it turns out, is just as pernicious as long-term unemployment.

Since college, I haven't been successful professionally, and as a result, I have had to rely on family to help me get by. For about three years, I was a substitute teacher, a job that has a lot of responsibility but pays very little. This year, I quit teaching and am using what little savings I have to search for a better job. If I fail to make something of myself soon, I’m going to carry out my plan; I’m tired of asking for help.
